labAnatomy.title: Interactive Brain Anatomy
labAnatomy.desc: Rotate, explode all, move and reset all in the 3D view — clicking a single part lets you rotate or reset only that part without changing the viewing angle; the 2D anatomy figure projects the real cortical surface (contour and partitions) with click, layer and label support; the sagittal section shows real medial-surface structure relationships.
labAnatomy.sectionDesc: Cut along the midsagittal plane: the cortex is the real medial-surface projection, showing the relative positions of the corpus callosum, thalamus, hippocampus, cerebellum and brainstem.
labAnatomy.regionFrontalInfo: The most anterior region, responsible for executive function, working memory, language production (Broca's area) and personality regulation — the core of cognitive control.
labAnatomy.regionParietalInfo: Posterior to the central sulcus; integrates somatosensation (touch, pain, proprioception) and spatial attention; the intraparietal sulcus is linked to visuomotor control.
labAnatomy.regionTemporalInfo: Below the lateral sulcus; processes hearing, language comprehension (Wernicke's area) and semantic memory; its medial part contains the hippocampus for episodic memory formation.
labAnatomy.regionOccipitalInfo: At the back of the brain; home of the visual cortex (V1–V5), where visual information is processed — the source of visual BCI paradigms such as SSVEP.
labAnatomy.regionCerebellumInfo: Behind the brainstem; coordinates movement, balance and procedural learning, and contributes to cognitive timing and fine motor control.
labAnatomy.regionBrainstemInfo: Connects the brain to the spinal cord; contains midbrain, pons and medulla, regulating breathing and heart rate; the ascending reticular activating system relates to arousal and attention.
labAnatomy.regionCorpusCallosumInfo: The white-matter bundle connecting the two hemispheres; damage causes 'split-brain' syndrome.
labAnatomy.regionThalamusInfo: The subcortical sensory relay — nearly all sensory input (except olfaction) passes through it to the cortex; also involved in attentional gating and sleep rhythms.
labAnatomy.regionHippocampusInfo: In the medial temporal lobe; key to episodic memory formation and spatial navigation; where long-term potentiation (LTP) has been studied most extensively.
labAnatomy.regionVentricleInfo: Brain cavities filled with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), providing cushioning, nutrients and waste clearance; abnormal CSF circulation is linked to several neurological disorders.
labAnatomy.regionNone: Click a region on the left to read about it, or toggle Layers / Labels / Section to explore different structures.

labCogsim.title: Cognitive Experiments
labCogsim.desc: Run three classic cognitive experiments yourself and learn what they tell us about the brain.
labCogsim.menuHint: Three classic paradigms — pick one to start. You can go back and switch at any time.
labCogsim.stroopDesc: When word meaning conflicts with ink color, responses slow down and errors increase — automatic semantic processing interferes with controlled color naming.
labCogsim.stroopHow: Each color word is printed in a different color. Judge the INK COLOR of the word, not its meaning.
labCogsim.stroopKeys: Keyboard: Q red · W blue · E green · R yellow (or click a swatch)
labCogsim.rtTooSoon: Too early — wait for the square to appear.
labCogsim.stroopCompared: Incongruent trials are usually 50–100 ms slower — that is the Stroop interference effect.
labCogsim.stroopNote: The effect implicates a conflict-monitoring system in prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate (ACC detects conflict, PFC resolves it).
labCogsim.rtDesc: Measuring the interval between stimulus onset and response — a basic index of cognitive processing speed.
labCogsim.rtKeys: Keyboard: press Space when the square appears (or click React)
labCogsim.rtSimpleHow: Tap 'React' as soon as the square appears.
labCogsim.rtChoiceHow: When the square appears, judge its color: tap RED for red, BLUE for blue.
labCogsim.rtCompared: Choice RT is typically 100–200 ms slower than simple RT — the difference reflects stimulus discrimination and response selection.
labCogsim.digitDesc: Watch a sequence of digits and recall them in order. Working-memory capacity is about 7±2 items.
labCogsim.digitHow: The digit sequence is shown briefly; then type the digits you remember, in order.
labCogsim.digitWrong: Not quite. Your span is about {n} digits.
labCogsim.digitDone: Done! Your digit span is about {n} digits.
labCogsim.digitNote: Span relates to the left prefrontal working-memory system and the phonological loop; chunking strategies can improve it.
labCogsim.stroopIdle: Click Start — trials appear one by one.
labCogsim.rtWait: Watch the center; wait for the square…

labSignals.title: Neural Signals & Paradigms
labSignals.desc: Canvas animations of EEG / ERP / P300 / SSVEP / motor-imagery waveforms and paradigms — to see where signals come from and how to read them.
labSignals.eegDesc: With eyes closed and relaxed, an 8–12 Hz alpha rhythm appears over occipital areas and is suppressed by opening the eyes or attending. Amplitudes are about 10–100 µV.
labSignals.eegHint: Alpha is the most visible EEG rhythm and a common target of neurofeedback training.
labSignals.erpDesc: Standard stimuli are presented repeatedly with occasional deviants; a deviant elicits a positive peak around 300 ms (P300), larger when attention is engaged.
labSignals.erpHint: P300 drives classic ERP-BCIs (e.g. the P300 speller): the attended row/column flash elicits a larger P300.
labSignals.ssvepDesc: Flickering a light source at a fixed rate drives a steady-state response in the occipital cortex at the same frequency (and harmonics); the frequency code can serve as BCI commands.
labSignals.ssvepHint: Two squares flicker at 8 Hz and 12 Hz; look at one and the spectrum shows a clear peak at its frequency.
labSignals.miDesc: Imagining limb movement (without executing it) desynchronizes mu (8–12 Hz) and beta (13–30 Hz) rhythms over the contralateral motor cortex — event-related desynchronization (ERD), the neural basis of motor-imagery BCIs.
labSignals.miHint: Compare the 'rest' and 'imagine' traces: oscillation amplitude drops markedly during imagery.
labSignals.canvasHint: Animated simulation, not a real recording; useful for understanding paradigms and waveform shapes.

labBci.title: BCI Case Studies
labBci.desc: Break representative BCI applications into six steps — problem, paradigm, signal, decoding, performance, limitations — to see how a real brain-computer interface is built.
labBci.case1Problem: Patients with paralysis or ALS cannot type; they need a muscle-independent character input.
labBci.case1Paradigm: A character matrix flashes rows/columns randomly (oddball paradigm); attended rows/columns elicit a larger P300.
labBci.case1Signal: Scalp EEG (Pz, Cz, Oz etc.); P300 is a positive peak ~300 ms after the stimulus.
labBci.case1Decode: Classify each flash as target or not — classic methods use SWLDA or LDA on averaged epochs, picking the highest discriminant score.
labBci.case1Perf: Reports of roughly 60–100% character accuracy (with repetitions), typing about 1–5 characters/min.
labBci.case1Limit: Requires gaze at the target (eye movement dependent); accuracy trades off against number of repetitions; P300 strength varies across people.
labBci.case2Desc: Several commands flicker at different frequencies; gazing at one selects it (dialing, wheelchair turning, game control).
labBci.case2Problem: A command-selection method with high information transfer rate (ITR) and low training burden.
labBci.case2Paradigm: Stimuli flicker at different rates (e.g. 8–15 Hz); the EEG shows a steady-state response at the attended frequency.
labBci.case2Signal: Scalp EEG (occipital O1/O2/Oz); CCA correlates EEG against frequency templates.
labBci.case2Decode: Canonical correlation analysis (CCA) / multi-channel CCA: correlate EEG with sine-cosine templates of each frequency; the max-correlation frequency is the attended target.
labBci.case2Perf: ITR often reaches 60–150 bit/min — among the highest throughputs of non-invasive BCIs.
labBci.case2Limit: Needs persistent flicker on screen (visual fatigue, photosensitive-epilepsy risk); gazing blocks other visual tasks.
labBci.case3Desc: Imagining left/right hand or feet movements is decoded into prosthetic commands.
labBci.case3Problem: Give amputees or patients with motor impairments intent-based (not muscle-based) control of prosthetics or exoskeletons.
labBci.case3Paradigm: The user imagines moving left hand, right hand or feet on cue; mu/beta rhythms over the contralateral motor cortex show ERD.
labBci.case3Signal: Scalp EEG (C3/C4/Cz motor electrodes); CSP (common spatial patterns) is widely used for spatial filtering.
labBci.case3Decode: CSP + LDA/SVM classifiers on power features extracted from the imagery window.
labBci.case3Perf: Binary (left vs right hand) accuracy around 70–90%; 4-class (hands/feet/tongue) 60–80%; high individual variability, 15–30% 'BCI-illiterate' users.
labBci.case3Limit: Large individual differences, needs calibration and training; feedback latency strongly affects controllability.
labBci.case4Desc: Intracortical microelectrode arrays record spikes and decode movement intent or attempted speech.
labBci.case4Problem: Patients with severe motor disability (high spinal cord injury, brainstem stroke) need high-precision continuous control (cursor/arm/speech).
labBci.case4Paradigm: The patient imagines arm movement or attempts to speak; intracortical microelectrodes (e.g. Utah arrays) record motor/sensory cortex activity.
labBci.case4Signal: Intracortical spikes and local field potentials (LFP) — spatial resolution far beyond scalp EEG.
labBci.case4Decode: Kalman filters or recurrent neural networks (RNN) decode neural activity into continuous kinematics (velocity/direction) or phoneme sequences.
labBci.case4Perf: Multi-joint arm control and 'brain-controlled speech' at tens of words/min have been demonstrated in clinical trials (BrainGate, speech-synthesis studies).
labBci.case4Limit: Requires invasive surgery (infection, electrode degradation); long-term stability and at-home usability remain key challenges.
labBci.takeaway: Takeaway: every BCI follows the same pipeline — problem → paradigm → signal → decoding → performance → limitations; the paradigm shapes the signal features and the decoder determines how well the information is recovered.

manual.title: User Guide
manual.lead: From looking up a term to running an experiment — what each entry point does, where your data lives, and the limits of the content.
manual.step1: Type a Chinese term, English word or abbreviation (e.g. P300, SSVEP, synapse) in the search box at the top and press Enter.
manual.step2: Open a term: read the one-line definition and plain explanation first, then the engineering notes and cited sources.
manual.step3: Open Study Tools to review with flashcards, spelling practice and quizzes; wrong answers go to your mistake book.
manual.step4: Open the Lab to rotate the 3D brain, run cognitive experiments, or explore neural signal and BCI pipeline simulations.
manual.step5: My Learning collects progress, favorites, mistakes and check-ins; by default everything stays in this browser.
manual.step6: To sync across devices, click Sign in at the top right. Every feature also works without an account.

manual.disclaimerBody: This site is for study reference only and does not constitute medical, diagnostic or treatment advice. AI generation, automated collection and human editing can all introduce errors; 3D models and simulations are teaching aids, not real measurements. For symptoms or clinical questions, consult a qualified professional.

The textbook baseline is docs/READING_LIST.md. When citing this site, verify the original source and edition.
manual.feedbackBody: Found an error, gap or unclear wording? Use the Feedback box at the top (page and screenshot welcome) or post in the Community. We review regularly and log corrections in the source registry.
